blocks.text: Line 20: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: The Krebs cycle is a stage of cellular respiration that breaks down fuel molecules and loads their electrons onto the carriers NADH and FADH2. These carriers then deliver the electrons to the electron transport chain, where most ATP is produced.

terms.definition: An electron carrier molecule that transports electrons to the electron transport chain.
An electron carrier, similar to NADH, made during the Krebs cycle.
A series of proteins that uses electrons to produce large amounts of ATP.

blocks.text: Line 21: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: Mitochondria are organelles where cellular respiration takes place. They convert energy stored in food into ATP, the cell's usable energy currency. Because they supply most of the cell's energy, they earned the nickname powerhouse of the cell.

terms.definition: Organelles that carry out cellular respiration to make ATP.
Adenosine triphosphate, the main energy currency cells use to do work.
The process of breaking down glucose to release energy as ATP.

blocks.text: Line 22: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: Photosynthesis is how plants capture light energy to build glucose from carbon dioxide and water. It happens inside chloroplasts, organelles containing the green pigment chlorophyll. This is why the note correctly places it in chloroplasts, not mitochondria.

terms.definition: The process of using light energy to make glucose from CO2 and water.
Plant organelles containing chlorophyll where photosynthesis happens.
The green pigment that absorbs light energy for photosynthesis.

blocks.text: Line 23: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: This repeats a key idea: the Krebs cycle's main job is charging up electron carriers. Each turn of the cycle generates NADH and FADH2, which later drop their electrons off at the electron transport chain to drive ATP production.

terms.definition: A cycle of reactions in respiration that produces electron carriers and some ATP.
An electron carrier that delivers electrons to the electron transport chain.
An electron carrier produced in the Krebs cycle.

blocks.text: Line 24: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: Same fact, worth remembering: cellular respiration finishes inside mitochondria, where the electron transport chain makes the bulk of ATP. Without mitochondria, cells would capture far less energy from glucose, so the powerhouse nickname fits their role well.

terms.definition: Organelles that perform cellular respiration and generate ATP.
The energy molecule cells use to power their activities.

blocks.text: Line 25: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: A common exam mix-up is swapping chloroplasts and mitochondria. Remember: chloroplasts capture light energy to build glucose (photosynthesis), while mitochondria break glucose down to release energy (respiration). Light is required for photosynthesis but not for respiration.

terms.definition: Organelles in plant cells where photosynthesis occurs.
Energy from sunlight that powers photosynthesis.

blocks.text: Line 26: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: Think of the Krebs cycle as a relay handoff: it does not make most ATP itself. Instead, it loads NADH and FADH2 with high-energy electrons and passes them to the electron transport chain, the final ATP-making stage.

terms.definition: Respiration stage that generates NADH and FADH2.
The final respiration stage that makes most ATP using electrons.

blocks.text: Line 27: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: This line links structure to function: mitochondria have folded inner membranes (cristae) that house the electron transport chain, allowing efficient ATP production. That is why cells needing lots of energy, like muscle cells, contain many mitochondria.

terms.definition: Folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane where respiration proteins sit.
The process that converts glucose energy into ATP.

blocks.text: Line 28: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: Photosynthesis needs light because chlorophyll in the chloroplast absorbs sunlight to power the reaction that converts carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen. Mitochondria cannot do this; they only handle the energy-releasing side, cellular respiration.

terms.definition: Light-powered process that builds glucose and releases oxygen.
Organelles where photosynthesis takes place.

blocks.text: Line 29: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: Repetition reinforces the pathway: glycolysis makes pyruvate, the Krebs cycle converts it and produces NADH and FADH2, and the electron transport chain uses those carriers to build most of the cell's ATP. Each stage depends on the previous one.

terms.definition: Electron carrier produced in the Krebs cycle.
Electron carrier that feeds electrons into the transport chain.

blocks.text: Line 30: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: ATP production is the reason mitochondria matter. Cellular respiration inside them extracts far more energy from each glucose molecule than glycolysis alone could, making mitochondria essential for energy-hungry processes like movement, growth, and active transport.

terms.definition: Organelles that generate ATP via cellular respiration.
Usable energy currency of the cell.

blocks.text: Line 31: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: Keep the division clear: chloroplasts are found mainly in leaf cells and perform photosynthesis using light, while mitochondria perform respiration in nearly all cells. Photosynthesis stores energy in glucose; respiration later releases that stored energy as ATP.

terms.definition: Light-capturing organelles where photosynthesis happens.
Sugar made during photosynthesis that stores energy.

blocks.text: Line 32: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: Note that the Krebs cycle also releases carbon dioxide as a waste product and makes a small amount of ATP directly. Its biggest contribution, though, is the NADH and FADH2 that power the electron transport chain.

terms.definition: Respiration stage producing carriers, CO2, and a little ATP.
Stage that converts carrier electrons into lots of ATP.

blocks.text: Line 33: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: This is a classic definition worth memorizing word for word. The cause-and-effect structure matters: mitochondria produce ATP (cause), which is why they are called the powerhouse (effect). Expect exam questions asking you to explain that link.

terms.definition: Organelles known as the powerhouse because they make ATP.
Glucose-breaking process that yields ATP.

blocks.text: Line 34: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: The phrase not mitochondria is a deliberate contrast to help you separate the two organelles. Photosynthesis is an energy-storing, light-dependent process in chloroplasts; respiration is an energy-releasing process in mitochondria. They are almost opposite reactions.

terms.definition: Light-dependent process that stores energy as glucose.
Organelles for respiration, not photosynthesis.

blocks.text: Line 35: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: FADH2 carries slightly less energy than NADH, so it yields a bit less ATP in the electron transport chain. Knowing that both carriers feed into the chain, but with different energy yields, is a common test detail.

terms.definition: High-energy electron carrier yielding more ATP.
Electron carrier yielding slightly less ATP than NADH.

blocks.text: Line 36: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: Connect this to the earlier lines: the NADH and FADH2 from the Krebs cycle travel to the mitochondrial inner membrane, where the electron transport chain uses them. So mitochondria are the powerhouse partly because they host that final stage.

terms.definition: Organelles hosting the Krebs cycle and electron transport chain.
Energy molecule produced mainly in mitochondria.

blocks.text: Line 37: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: Without light, photosynthesis stops because chlorophyll has no energy to absorb. Plants then rely only on respiration, burning stored glucose in mitochondria. This shows why the light requirement and the chloroplast location go together in this fact.

terms.definition: Pigment that absorbs light for photosynthesis.
Organelles containing chlorophyll, site of photosynthesis.

blocks.text: Line 38: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: One more pass to lock it in: the Krebs cycle runs in the mitochondrial matrix, and its NADH and FADH2 output is the crucial link between the early stages of respiration and the ATP-rich electron transport chain.

terms.definition: Innermost compartment of mitochondria where the Krebs cycle occurs.
Membrane pathway that turns electron carriers into ATP.

blocks.text: Line 39: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: Final takeaway tying the note together: mitochondria combine the Krebs cycle and the electron transport chain in one organelle, making them the main ATP factories. Chloroplasts, by contrast, make the glucose that respiration later breaks down.

terms.definition: Organelles that produce most cellular ATP.
Process converting glucose into ATP energy.

blocks.text: Line 40: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: This statement is correct. Photosynthesis happens inside chloroplasts, the green organelles in plant cells, and it needs light energy to turn carbon dioxide and water into glucose. Mitochondria do respiration instead, so the contrast made here is accurate.

terms.definition: Green organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place.
Process that uses light energy to make glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
Organelles that produce ATP through cellular respiration.

blocks.text: Line 41: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: Correct. The Krebs cycle, running in the mitochondrial matrix, loads captured energy onto the carriers NADH and FADH2. These carriers then deliver high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain, which uses them to make most of the cell's ATP.

terms.definition: Series of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix that extracts energy from food.
Electron carrier that delivers high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain.
Electron carrier, similar to NADH, that feeds electrons into the electron transport chain.

blocks.text: Line 42: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: Correct. Mitochondria perform cellular respiration, transferring energy from food into ATP, the cell's usable energy currency. Because they supply most of that ATP, they earned the nickname 'powerhouse of the cell.' This is a standard, accurate biology summary.

terms.definition: Adenosine triphosphate, the main energy currency cells use to power work.
Process that breaks down glucose to release energy stored as ATP.

blocks.text: Line 43: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: This repeats line 40 exactly. The fact is still correct: chloroplasts host photosynthesis and capture light energy, while mitochondria handle respiration. Repetition can help memory, but consider condensing duplicates to keep your notes tidy and easier to review.

terms.definition: Green organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place.
Light-powered process that builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water.

blocks.text: Line 44: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: This is an exact repeat of line 41. The content remains accurate: the Krebs cycle generates NADH and FADH2, which shuttle electrons to the electron transport chain. Repeating key facts can reinforce learning, though trimming duplicates saves space.

terms.definition: Reaction series in the mitochondrial matrix that extracts energy from food.
Protein chain that uses electron energy to produce ATP.

blocks.text: Line 45: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: This duplicates line 42. The statement is correct: mitochondria generate ATP through cellular respiration, which is why they are called the powerhouse of the cell. Consider removing repeated lines or grouping them into one summary section instead.

terms.definition: Main energy currency of the cell.
Process that breaks down glucose to release energy as ATP.

blocks.text: Line 46: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: Third repetition of the photosynthesis fact. It stays correct: chloroplasts, not mitochondria, carry out photosynthesis, and light energy is essential. If you keep duplicates intentionally for drilling, that is fine; otherwise consolidate them into one clear statement.

terms.definition: Green organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis happens.
Energy from sunlight that powers photosynthesis.

blocks.text: Line 47: The Krebs cycle produces NADH and FADH2 for the electron transport chain.
blocks.explanation: Another exact copy of the Krebs cycle line. The science is right: NADH and FADH2 made in the Krebs cycle feed electrons into the electron transport chain. Repetition aids recall, but a single well-written line usually suffices.

terms.definition: Electron carrier that delivers high-energy electrons to the electron transport chain.
Electron carrier that also feeds electrons into the electron transport chain.

blocks.text: Line 48: Mitochondria are the powerhouse of the cell because they produce ATP through cellular respiration.
blocks.explanation: This repeats the mitochondria statement once more. It is accurate: cellular respiration in mitochondria produces ATP, justifying the 'powerhouse' label. Multiple copies add no new information, so consider deleting extras or turning them into flashcards instead.

terms.definition: Organelles that produce ATP through cellular respiration.
Main energy currency of the cell.

blocks.text: Line 49: Photosynthesis occurs in chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and requires light energy.
blocks.explanation: Fourth copy of the photosynthesis line. The fact remains correct: chloroplasts perform photosynthesis using light energy, while mitochondria do not. For cleaner notes, keep one instance and use the freed space for new details or examples.

terms.definition: Light-powered process that builds glucose from carbon dioxide and water.
Green organelle in plant cells where photosynthesis takes place.

In chloroplasts, not mitochondria, and it requires light energy.
